1331.title: The best to their families
1331.hook: wonderful in public, tired at home, and a hadith that turns the measure around
1331.howItsDone: Muslims cite the hadith "the best of you are the best to their families" when speaking of marriage and home, and teachers use Salman's words to Abu al-Darda' to say that worship should not crowd out the rights of family.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the verse in al-Rum, and your line, dwell in tranquillity. Today, a sentence that measures a person by how they are at home.

Some people are wonderful in public. Patient with strangers, generous at work, the easiest person at any gathering. Then they get home, and the patience has been spent somewhere else. Short answers. A closed door. A hadith in Jami' at-Tirmidhi takes that pattern and turns the measure around. It doesn't ask how a person is at the mosque, or the office, or online. It asks about the people who see them tired, hungry, and in their oldest clothes.
screen: `WONDERFUL IN PUBLIC.` → `SPENT BY THE TIME THEY'RE HOME.` → `THE MEASURE, TURNED AROUND.`

segments.voice: The hadith, in paraphrase: the best of you are those who are best to their families, and I am the best of you to my family. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says it about himself, and sets home as the measure. The word for family here is ahl: your household, your people. Second, a story in Sahih al-Bukhari. The companion Salman al-Farisi visits his brother in faith, Abu al-Darda', and finds his wife, Umm al-Darda', looking neglected. She tells him, in paraphrase: your brother has no need of this world. Abu al-Darda' is fasting, and at night he means to pray straight through. Salman makes him eat. When night comes, he tells him to sleep, and late in the night wakes him, and they pray together. Then Salman says, in paraphrase: your Lord has a right over you, your own self has a right over you, and your family has a right over you, so give each one its due. When they tell the Prophet, he answers: Salman has spoken the truth. Third, notice whose concern starts the story: a wife, whose husband's devotion had left no room for her. The hadith takes her side, and it does it in the name of worship, not against it. Fourth, what best looks like. Not grand. Eating together. Sleeping enough to be kind in the morning. Giving the people at home the patience you'd give a guest. Another hadith in at-Tirmidhi, in paraphrase: the most complete of the believers in faith are the best of them in character, and the best of you are the best to their wives. Character, measured at the kitchen table.
screen: `THE BEST OF YOU: BEST TO THEIR FAMILY.` · `SALMAN VISITS ABU AL-DARDA'.` · `GIVE EACH ONE ITS DUE.` · `CHARACTER, AT THE KITCHEN TABLE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the people at home, or the family you have, near or far: who has seen you at your most tired lately? Pick one small thing you could do for them, a meal, a call, a chore done before anyone asks, a stretch of full attention with nothing in your hands, and picture their face when it happens.
The best to their families. A hadith that measures a person at home, among the people who see them tired. Today's word.
screen: `THE BEST TO THEIR FAMILIES — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: best at home. The people who see you tired are the measure. Glad you came today.

1332.title: Home life
1332.hook: someone asked 'A'ishah what he did at home; she said he served his family, and when the prayer came, he went to pray
1332.howItsDone: Muslims point to 'A'ishah's description of the Prophet at home, serving his family and mending his own clothes, as a model for household life, and to his going out when the time for prayer came.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the best to their families, and your line, best at home. Today, what that looked like on an ordinary day.

A question put to 'A'ishah, and kept in Sahih al-Bukhari. Someone asked her what the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, used to do in his house. Not in the mosque. Not on the battlefield, not on the pulpit. In the house. It's the kind of thing you'd only ask the person who lived with him. Her answer is short. He used to be busy serving his family, she said, and when the time for prayer came, he went out to the prayer. No speech. A man at home doing the work of the home, until the call came.
screen: `WHAT DID HE DO AT HOME?` → `ASK THE ONE WHO LIVED WITH HIM.` → `SERVING HIS FAMILY.`

segments.voice: Look at the order in her answer: first the family, then the prayer. Not because the prayer mattered less. When its time came, he went, and the serving stopped. But until then, the house had his hands. The word in the Arabic report is mihnah, the work of the household, the everyday labor of a home. Other reports fill in the picture. In one kept in the Musnad of Ahmad, 'A'ishah is asked again, and she says, in paraphrase, that he mended his own clothes, repaired his own sandal, and did what any man does in his house. A man the Qur'an calls a messenger, sewing a torn garment himself. Now put that next to yesterday's hadith: the best of you are the best to their families. The serving is what that sentence looks like on a Tuesday. A shirt. A sandal strap. Whatever needs doing. And the second half of her answer keeps the serving from swallowing everything. The home was not a reason to miss the prayer, and the prayer was not a reason to skip the home. Some readers hear in this a rhythm for a whole life: the small work of love, then the turn toward Allah, then back again. The house and the prayer aren't rivals. They take turns. The prayer, when he left for it, was not an escape from the dishes. It was the next thing in the same day.
screen: `FIRST THE FAMILY, THEN THE PRAYER.` · `MIHNAH, THE WORK OF THE HOUSE.` · `HE MENDED HIS OWN CLOTHES.` · `THE HOUSE AND THE PRAYER TAKE TURNS.`

segments.voice: Let your mind walk through the place you live: the sink, the laundry, the thing that's been broken for a week. Pick one small job you'd normally leave for someone else, and see yourself doing it start to finish, without telling anyone. Then see yourself turning toward the next thing in your day; if you pray, let that be the next prayer, whenever its time comes.
Home life. In 'A'ishah's answer: he served his family, mended his clothes, and when prayer came, went to pray. Today's word.
Your line: serve, then pray. A sandal strap, and then the call. Rest well.

1333.title: Parents as shepherds
1333.hook: each of you is a shepherd, and each of you will be asked about the flock
1333.howItsDone: Muslims often cite the hadith that each person is a shepherd responsible for their flock when speaking about parents' duties, describing children as a trust rather than a possession.

segments.voice: Yesterday: home life, and your line, serve, then pray. Today, the people in the house who are still small.

Count the people you'd have to answer for. At dusk, a shepherd does exactly that: one, two, three, all the way through the flock, because if one is missing, the whole evening changes. A report in Sahih al-Bukhari says the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, once tended sheep himself, for the people of Makkah. So when he described responsibility, he reached for a picture he knew from the inside. Not a king, not a judge. A shepherd, who walks behind the flock all day and at the end of it has to answer for every one.
screen: `AT DUSK, THE SHEPHERD COUNTS.` → `HE TENDED SHEEP HIMSELF.` → `ANSWER FOR EVERY ONE.`

segments.voice: The hadith is kept in al-Bukhari, from 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar. In paraphrase: each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is responsible for his flock. Then it goes down a list. The ruler is a shepherd over his people. A man is a shepherd over his household. A woman is a shepherd over her husband's house and his children. A servant is a shepherd over his master's property. And it ends where it began: each of you is a shepherd, and each of you is responsible for his flock. The Arabic word is ra'i, the one who tends, and the flock is ra'iyyah, those who are tended. Notice what that word doesn't say. A shepherd doesn't own the sheep in this picture. Someone else does. The shepherd is trusted with them, and will be asked. Some readers hear in that the difference between possession and trust. A child, in this frame, isn't a project or a trophy. A child is a flock you were handed, and the question at the end isn't how impressive they turned out. It's how you tended them. And look at who's on the list. Mother and father both. The ruler, and the servant too. Nobody is only a sheep; even the least powerful person in the hadith has something in their care. The Qur'an puts the same weight on the home in surah al-Tahrim, telling believers, in paraphrase, to guard themselves and their families from the Fire. Tending begins at home, and a shepherd's main tool, every day, is simply being there.
screen: `EACH OF YOU IS A SHEPHERD.` · `RA'I: THE ONE WHO TENDS.` · `NOT OWNER, BUT TRUSTED.` · `NOBODY IS ONLY A SHEEP.`

segments.voice: Think of a child in your life, your own, a niece or nephew, a student, or anyone in your care, and picture what they're into right now and what they keep trying to tell you. See yourself giving them ten unhurried minutes: no phone, no correcting, just attention. If you pray, hold them in your prayer for a moment.
Parents as shepherds. In the hadith, everyone is a shepherd over someone, trusted with them, and asked about them. Today's word.
Your line: each a shepherd. Trusted, not owning, and asked at the end of the day. Same time tomorrow.

1334.title: Honoring the elders
1334.hook: he is not one of us who shows no mercy to the young and no respect to the old
1334.howItsDone: Muslims are taught to honor parents and elders, citing surah 17:23–24 and hadith that honoring the old is part of glorifying Allah, and treat visiting and serving elders as part of the faith.

segments.voice: Yesterday: parents as shepherds, and your line, each a shepherd. Today the flock turns around: the ones who once tended us.

"Fie." That's the word Pickthall chose, in his translation of the Qur'an, for a small sound of irritation. A sigh with a word in it. The kind of noise that slips out when an aging parent asks the same question for the third time, or takes too long at the door, or tells the story you've heard before. The Qur'an, in surah Bani Isra'il, forbids exactly that sound. Not shouting. Not cruelty. Just the little huff. That's how close the line is drawn around the old.
screen: `"FIE."` → `A SMALL SOUND OF IRRITATION.` → `FORBIDDEN, AROUND THE OLD.`

segments.voice: Here are the words, in Pickthall's translation of 17:23: "If one of them or both of them attain old age with thee, say not "Fie" unto them nor repulse them, but speak unto them a gracious word." With thee. Some readers hear in that a parent growing old in your house, in your care. The next verse adds the posture: lower to them the wing of humility, out of mercy, and pray for them, as they cared for you when you were little. Then the hadith widens the circle from parents to every elder. In al-Tirmidhi, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says, in paraphrase: he is not one of us who does not show mercy to our young and does not honor our old. Not one of us. Strong words, set beside ordinary acts. And a hadith in Abu Dawud goes further: honoring a gray-haired Muslim is part of glorifying Allah. Gray hair, in that picture, isn't something to hide or hurry past. It's a reason for respect. Notice how the Tirmidhi hadith holds the young and the old together. Mercy goes down, to the small. Honor goes up, to the old. And the person in the middle of life, busy, tired, impatient, is the one being spoken to. The elder at the end of the table may be slow. The verse doesn't ask you to pretend otherwise. It asks for the gracious word anyway.
screen: `SAY NOT "FIE" UNTO THEM.` · `LOWER THE WING OF HUMILITY.` · `MERCY DOWN, HONOR UP.` · `GRAY HAIR, A REASON FOR RESPECT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone older in your life: a parent, a grandparent, an old neighbor, a retired teacher, someone at the mosque or down the hall. Think of one question to ask them about their own life, and picture listening to the whole answer, even if you've heard it before. If you pray, remember them in your prayer.
Honoring the elders. No sigh, no brushing off; the gracious word, the lowered wing, respect for the gray hair. Today's word.
Your line: honor the gray hair. The gracious word, even when they're slow. Thanks for sitting with this one.

1335.title: Visiting the sick
1335.hook: whoever visits the sick is in the harvest of the garden until he returns
1335.howItsDone: Muslims visit the sick at home and in hospital as a sunnah, often bringing food and making a short supplication for the person's healing, citing the hadith that the visitor is in the harvest of the garden until they return.

segments.voice: Yesterday: honoring the elders, and your line, honor the gray hair. Today a new stretch of the life cycle begins: illness, and then death.

On the Day of Rising, in a hadith in Sahih Muslim, Allah speaks to a person, and the words are strange. I was sick, He says, and you did not visit Me. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, tells it. The person is baffled. My Lord, how could I visit You, when You are the Lord of the worlds? The answer comes back, in paraphrase: did you not know that My servant so-and-so was sick, and you did not visit him? Had you visited him, you would have found Me with him.
screen: `I WAS SICK, AND YOU DID NOT VISIT ME.` → `HOW COULD I VISIT YOU?` → `YOU WOULD HAVE FOUND ME WITH HIM.`

segments.voice: The word is 'iyadah, visiting the sick. The hadith in Muslim keeps going, and it widens. I asked you for food, and you did not feed Me. I asked you for water, and you did not give Me to drink. Each time the same bafflement, and each time the same answer: My servant asked you. Had you done it, you would have found it with Me. A different hadith in Muslim gives the visit its picture. Whoever visits a sick person, the Prophet said, remains in the khurfah of the garden until he returns. Someone asked what the khurfah was. The answer: its harvest, its fruit being gathered. So the walk to the hospital, the time in the plastic chair, the walk back to the car, all of it, in this picture, is time spent picking fruit in Paradise. Al-Bukhari keeps a short command that puts it next to other basic duties, in paraphrase: feed the hungry, visit the sick, and set the captive free. Notice what the visit doesn't require. No cure. No perfect words. You're not asked to fix anything. You're asked to show up, sit near, and go home. Bring nothing but yourself, if that's all you have. The harvest starts at the door.
screen: `'IYADAH: VISITING THE SICK.` · `FOOD, WATER, AND A VISIT.` · `THE KHURFAH: THE GARDEN'S HARVEST.` · `NO CURE NEEDED, JUST COME.`

segments.voice: Who do you know who is sick right now, in the hospital, recovering at home, or living with an illness people have stopped asking about? Let one face come, think how you could reach them, a visit, a call, a message, and find a simple first sentence: how are you, really? If you pray, ask for their healing in your own words.
'Iyadah. Visiting the sick: a visit that, in the hadith, keeps you in the garden's harvest until you come home. Today's word.
Your line: the garden's harvest. Every step to the bedside, in that picture, is fruit being gathered. Until next time.

1336.title: Illness as expiation
1336.hook: no tiredness, illness or worry touches a believer, not even a thorn's prick, without wiping away some sins
1336.howItsDone: Muslims who are ill often recall the hadith that illness and even a thorn's prick wipe away sins, and pair patience with seeking medical treatment, which the hadith also encourage.

segments.voice: Yesterday: 'iyadah, visiting the sick, and your line, the garden's harvest. Today, the same bedside, seen from the bed.

A thorn. Small enough to pull out with your fingernails, sharp enough to make you say ow. It's in a hadith, kept in Sahih al-Bukhari, and it's the smallest thing on a list. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, names what can happen to a believer: tiredness, illness, worry, sorrow, harm, distress. And then he goes all the way down, to the prick of a thorn. Even that, he says, is not for nothing. Today is about why.
screen: `A THORN.` → `THE SMALLEST THING ON THE LIST.` → `EVEN THAT, NOT FOR NOTHING.`

segments.voice: Here's the hadith, in paraphrase. No tiredness, no illness, no worry, no sorrow, no harm and no distress befalls a Muslim, even the prick of a thorn, without Allah wiping away some of his sins by it. The word for that is kaffarah, expiation. In this picture, the hard hours of being sick are not empty hours. Something is happening in them, even when the person lying there can do nothing at all. Al-Bukhari keeps a story that shows how this was lived. Ibn 'Abbas once pointed out a woman to a student and said: shall I show you a woman of the people of Paradise? She had come to the Prophet with an illness that made her fall in fits, and asked him to pray for her cure. He gave her a choice. If you wish, be patient, and you will have Paradise. Or if you wish, I will pray to Allah to heal you. She chose patience. But she asked for one thing: that when the fits came, she wouldn't be uncovered. And he prayed for that. Now the other side, so the picture isn't bent. Patience here doesn't mean refusing a doctor. A hadith in Abu Dawud says, in paraphrase, that Allah sent down both disease and its remedy, so seek treatment. The medicine and the patience aren't rivals. You take the pills. You wait for the results. And the waiting, in this hadith, counts too.

1337.title: Remembering death
1337.hook: remember often the destroyer of pleasures, said the Prophet; and a week of home, elders and the sick ends here
1337.howItsDone: Muslims are encouraged to remember death often, citing the hadith of the destroyer of pleasures and the Qur'an's "Every soul will taste of death"; some visit graves for this reason.

segments.voice: Yesterday: illness as expiation, and your line, nothing is wasted. Today the week closes with the thought underneath all of it.

Why would anyone think about death on purpose? In a hadith kept by al-Tirmidhi, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says something that would sound almost rude at a party. Remember often, he said, the destroyer of pleasures. He meant death. Not as a threat. As a remembering, brought to mind in the middle of ordinary life: a good meal, a long laugh with friends, a new thing finally in your hands. This week walked from the home, to the elders, to the sickbed. Today it reaches the place every one of those roads ends.
screen: `WHY THINK OF DEATH ON PURPOSE?` → `REMEMBER THE DESTROYER OF PLEASURES.` → `WHERE EVERY ROAD ENDS.`

segments.voice: The Qur'an says it plainly, in Pickthall's translation of surah Al 'Imran: "Every soul will taste of death." No exceptions in the sentence. So what is the remembering for? The hadith gives one clue in its own wording: it destroys pleasures. Some readers take that not as ruining every good thing, but as cutting through the ones that have grown too large. The argument you're still nursing. The thing you'd do anything to own. Death, remembered for a moment, shrinks them back to size. Another hadith, in al-Bukhari, gives the posture. The Prophet took 'Abdullah ibn 'Umar by the shoulder and told him, in paraphrase: be in this world as though you were a stranger, or a traveler passing through. And Ibn 'Umar used to say: when evening comes, don't wait for the morning, and when morning comes, don't wait for the evening. A traveler doesn't hate the road. A traveler just doesn't unpack everything. Now look back over this week through that lens. Serving at home, in 'A'ishah's report. Tending the flock you were given. The gracious word to the old. The visit to the sick. The patience in the hard hours. Each of those is something a traveler would want done before the road ends. Remembering death, in this teaching, isn't gloom. It's what makes today's small kindness urgent.
screen: `EVERY SOUL WILL TASTE OF DEATH.` · `IT SHRINKS THINGS BACK TO SIZE.` · `A STRANGER, OR A TRAVELER.` · `IT MAKES THE SMALL KINDNESS URGENT.`

segments.voice: Without drama, let yourself remember that this life has an end, as every life does, and stay with that gently for a few breaths. Then ask: if the road were shorter than I think, what from this week would I want to have done, a visit, a call, an apology, a job at home? If you pray, turn that answer into your prayer. And if thoughts of death ever feel heavy or close, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or call local emergency help.
Remembering death. Bringing the end to mind on purpose, often, so the small things shrink and the good ones get done. Today's word.
Your line: remember the end. A traveler on the road doesn't unpack everything. That's the week, and thank you for walking it.
